The study employs dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to investigate the optical conductivity of a single doped hole in the Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model. This model combines the effects of strong electronic correlations, represented by the \(t\)-\(J\) framework, with electron–phonon coupling, described by the Holstein interaction. It is therefore well suited for studying how a charge carrier moves through an antiferromagnetic background while simultaneously interacting with lattice vibrations.

A key result of the work is the derivation of an exact solution for the optical conductivity in the limit of infinite connectivity. In this limit, the DMFT approach becomes exact, allowing the authors to treat both magnetic interactions and local electron–phonon coupling in a controlled way. The solution reveals how the motion of a single hole is strongly renormalized by its coupling to spin excitations and phonons, leading to the formation of polaronic states.

The analysis is then applied to the electron-doped cuprate compound Nd\(_{2-x}\)Ce\(_x\)CuO\(_4\). By comparing the theoretical optical conductivity with experimental observations, the study shows that many characteristic features of the material’s optical response can be understood within the Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) framework. In particular, the model accounts for the redistribution of optical spectral weight and the emergence of broad absorption structures.

Overall, the work demonstrates that the optical conductivity of Nd\(_{2-x}\)Ce\(_x\)CuO\(_4\) can be interpreted in terms of the formation of both magnetic and lattice polarons. The doped carrier becomes dressed by distortions of the surrounding spin background as well as by local lattice deformations, and these combined effects play a central role in shaping the observed optical spectra.
outputs.L4:
Dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) is employed to investigate the optical conductivity of a single doped hole in the Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model. This model combines the motion of a charge carrier in an antiferromagnetic spin background, described by the \(t\)-\(J\) Hamiltonian, with a local coupling to dispersionless lattice vibrations of Holstein type. It therefore provides a natural framework for studying the simultaneous influence of magnetic correlations and electron-phonon interactions on the dynamics of a doped carrier in a strongly correlated system.

An exact solution is obtained in the limit of infinite lattice connectivity, where DMFT becomes exact and the many-body problem can be mapped onto an effective local impurity problem embedded in a self-consistent bath. Within this approach, the optical conductivity is calculated for different values of the exchange interaction, phonon frequency, temperature, and electron-phonon coupling strength. The results show how the hole can become dressed by both spin excitations and lattice distortions, leading to the formation of magnetic, lattice, or combined spin-lattice polarons. These polaronic effects strongly reshape the optical response, producing broad absorption bands, shifts of spectral weight, and characteristic mid-infrared features.

The theory is then applied to the electron-doped cuprate compound Nd\(_{2-x}\)Ce\(_x\)CuO\(_4\), focusing on the optical-conductivity spectra observed in the lightly doped regime. The calculated spectra reproduce many of the main experimental features, including the position and shape of broad absorption peaks and their evolution with temperature and coupling strength. The comparison indicates that neither magnetic effects nor lattice effects alone are sufficient to account for the observed behavior. Instead, the optical response is best understood as arising from a carrier strongly coupled to both the antiferromagnetic background and local lattice distortions.

This analysis highlights the importance of coupled spin-lattice polaron formation in the optical properties of doped Mott insulators. In Nd\(_{2-x}\)Ce\(_x\)CuO\(_4\), the observed conductivity features can be interpreted as signatures of a doped carrier whose motion is hindered by magnetic disorder and further renormalized by phonon coupling. The Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model treated within DMFT therefore provides a unified description of the interplay between strong electronic correlations, antiferromagnetism, and electron-phonon interaction in this material.
outputs.L5:
Holstein and CuO systems are important topics in condensed matter physics, especially in the study of electron–phonon interactions and strongly correlated materials. The Holstein model describes how electrons interact with local lattice vibrations, or phonons. This interaction can lead to the formation of polarons, where an electron becomes coupled to a distortion of the surrounding lattice. Such effects are significant in understanding electrical conductivity, charge transport, and metal–insulator transitions.

CuO, or copper(II) oxide, is a transition metal oxide with strong electronic correlations and complex magnetic properties. It has attracted interest because copper oxides are closely related to high-temperature superconducting materials. In CuO, the interaction between charge carriers, lattice vibrations, and magnetic ordering can strongly influence the material’s physical behavior.

When the Holstein model is applied to CuO or related copper oxide systems, it can help explain how lattice distortions affect electron motion. This is especially useful for studying polaron formation, charge localization, and the role of phonons in correlated oxides. Understanding these interactions is essential for developing better theoretical models of copper-based materials and may contribute to future advances in electronic and superconducting technologies.

counterfactuals.output: We study the optical conductivity of a single doped hole in the Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model using dynamical mean-field theory, incorporating both strong antiferromagnetic spin correlations and local electron–phonon coupling. The method provides a nonperturbative description of charge dynamics in the regime relevant to lightly doped Mott insulators, allowing the evolution of phonon-assisted absorption features and magnetic sidebands to be tracked as a function of coupling strength and temperature. Applying the approach to electron-doped Nd\(_{2-x}\)Ce\(_x\)CuO\(_4\), we show that the calculated optical spectra capture key features of the experimentally observed mid-infrared response. The results indicate that the optical conductivity arises from the combined effects of spin-polaron formation and lattice dressing, emphasizing the importance of treating magnetic and phononic interactions on equal footing in cuprate charge dynamics.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that solves $\sigma(\omega)$ for one hole in the Holstein-t-J model in the infinite-connectivity limit and relates the results to optical conductivity experiments in electron-doped cuprates.
counterfactuals.output:
The study analyzes the optical conductivity, \(\sigma(\omega)\), of a single charge carrier moving in an antiferromagnetic background while also coupling locally to lattice vibrations. The model is the Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model in the infinite-connectivity limit, which makes the one-hole problem essentially solvable through local Green’s functions/continued-fraction methods and removes vertex corrections in the optical response.

## Model and physical question

The Hamiltonian combines:

\[
H_{tJ} = -t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}
\left(\tilde c^\dagger_{i\sigma}\tilde c_{j\sigma}+h.c.\right)
+J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}
\left(\mathbf S_i\cdot \mathbf S_j-\frac14 n_i n_j\right),
\]

with a local Holstein coupling,

\[
H_{\text{ep}} = \omega_0\sum_i b_i^\dagger b_i
+ g\sum_i n_i^h\left(b_i^\dagger+b_i\right),
\]

where \(n_i^h\) is the hole density, \(\omega_0\) is an optical phonon frequency, and \(g\) is the electron-phonon coupling.

The central problem is how a single doped carrier absorbs light when its motion is hindered both by:

1. antiferromagnetic spin correlations, which create a “string” of spin defects as the carrier moves, and  
2. lattice distortions, which can dress the carrier into a polaron.

The goal is to compute \(\sigma(\omega)\) and compare the resulting mid-infrared optical structures with those observed in electron-doped cuprates.

## Infinite-connectivity solution

In the infinite-connectivity or large-coordination limit, the carrier’s motion becomes retraceable: when the hole moves away from its original site it creates a string of spin defects, and the energetics of that string can be treated exactly in a local framework. The same limit also simplifies the optical conductivity, because vertex corrections vanish or become tractable.

The optical conductivity is obtained from the Kubo formula. In this limit it can be expressed in terms of local one-particle propagators, giving a controlled way to include both magnetic and phonon dressing of the carrier. The resulting spectra show how the absorption evolves as the exchange energy \(J\), phonon frequency \(\omega_0\), temperature, and electron-phonon coupling strength are varied.

## Main theoretical results

The study finds that the optical response is not well described by a purely magnetic \(t\)-\(J\) picture or by a purely Holstein small-polaron picture alone. Instead, the mid-infrared absorption arises from the combined effect of antiferromagnetic correlations and electron-phonon coupling.

Key results include:

- For weak electron-phonon coupling, the optical conductivity is dominated by magnetic excitations associated with the motion of the carrier in the antiferromagnetic background.
- Increasing the Holstein coupling transfers spectral weight into broad phonon-assisted sidebands.
- At intermediate coupling, the carrier behaves as a magneto-elastic polaron: it is dressed simultaneously by spin defects and local lattice distortions.
- The optical spectrum develops a broad mid-infrared band rather than a sharp quasiparticle-like absorption.
- The position and width of the mid-infrared peak depend sensitively on both \(J\) and the electron-phonon coupling.
- Temperature tends to broaden the spectra and shift optical weight, reflecting the weakening of antiferromagnetic correlations and the enhanced role of phonon fluctuations.

A central conclusion is that moderate electron-phonon coupling, when added to the \(t\)-\(J\) model, can strongly reshape the optical response even if the coupling is not large enough to produce a fully localized small polaron.

## Relation to electron-doped cuprates

The study connects the calculation to optical conductivity measurements in electron-doped cuprates such as

\[
\mathrm{Nd}_{2-x}\mathrm{Ce}_x\mathrm{CuO}_4
\]

and related compounds.

Experimentally, lightly doped electron-doped cuprates show:

- a broad mid-infrared absorption band,
- a transfer of optical spectral weight with doping and temperature,
- suppression of low-frequency conductivity in the insulating or underdoped regime,
- and features that cannot be explained by a simple Drude metal.

The calculated Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) spectra reproduce several qualitative aspects of these measurements. In particular, the broad mid-infrared band is interpreted as the optical excitation of a carrier dressed by both spin and lattice degrees of freedom. The antiferromagnetic exchange scale \(J\) sets the magnetic contribution to the absorption energy, while the Holstein coupling and phonon frequency control the phonon sidebands and the broadening of the response.

Thus, the study argues that the mid-infrared optical conductivity in electron-doped cuprates is evidence for a carrier that is not simply a free quasiparticle, but a composite object coupled to both antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations and lattice distortions.

## Overall conclusion

The work shows that solving the one-hole Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model in the infinite-connectivity limit gives a natural explanation for the mid-infrared optical conductivity of electron-doped cuprates. The main message is that optical experiments are best understood in terms of a magneto-elastic polaron: a doped carrier whose dynamics are controlled jointly by the antiferromagnetic background and electron-phonon interaction.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise research-paper abstract about magnetic and lattice polaron effects on optical conductivity in Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$ using DMFT.
counterfactuals.output: We study the optical conductivity of electron-doped Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$ using dynamical mean-field theory applied to a correlated electron model coupled to both spin and lattice degrees of freedom. Magnetic polaron formation, driven by carrier motion in an antiferromagnetic background, and lattice polaron effects from electron–phonon coupling are treated on the same footing. The calculated spectra reproduce key features observed experimentally, including mid-infrared absorption, spectral-weight transfer with doping, and the evolution toward a more coherent low-energy response. Magnetic correlations dominate the redistribution of optical spectral weight near the antiferromagnetic phase, while lattice coupling enhances carrier localization and broadens the mid-infrared band. With increasing Ce concentration, polaronic signatures weaken as electronic coherence develops and antiferromagnetic correlations are reduced. These results indicate that the optical response of Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$ reflects the combined influence of magnetic and lattice polarons, providing a unified interpretation of doping-dependent conductivity in electron-doped cuprates.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an APS-style abstract for a paper titled “Optical conductivity of the Holstein-t-J model in infinite dimensions” including DMFT, one-hole physics, and magnetic/lattice polaron formation.
counterfactuals.output: We study the optical conductivity of the Holstein-\(t\)-\(J\) model in the limit of infinite spatial dimensions using dynamical mean-field theory. Focusing on the one-hole regime, we analyze the interplay between exchange-induced magnetic correlations and local electron-phonon coupling in the formation of composite quasiparticles. In the absence of lattice coupling, the doped hole forms a magnetic polaron whose optical response reflects the ladder of string-like spin excitations generated by its motion in an antiferromagnetic background. Coupling to dispersionless Holstein phonons produces lattice-polaron dressing, leading to spectral-weight redistribution, phonon sidebands, and a strong suppression of the low-frequency optical response. We show that the optical conductivity provides a sensitive probe of the crossover from predominantly magnetic to predominantly lattice polaron behavior, as controlled by the exchange interaction, phonon frequency, temperature, and electron-phonon coupling strength. Within DMFT, vertex corrections vanish in infinite dimensions, allowing the conductivity to be expressed directly in terms of local one-particle spectral functions. Our results clarify how spin and lattice degrees of freedom cooperate or compete in determining charge dynamics in strongly correlated systems and provide a benchmark for interpreting mid-infrared optical features in lightly doped Mott insulators.
